#4174. Heartopia goes to the movies with its next event

Heartopia's Whale Island will soon host a new event that's all about the magic of cinema.

Heartopia’s next in-game event has been announced, and it’s one you may not have seen coming. Developer XD Games revealed Dreamlight Cinematics Festival, an upcoming limited-time event that celebrates cinema and movie-making.

Dreamlight Cinematics kicks off March 21, and will run through May 1, available across the game’s PC and mobile versions.

Dreamlight Cinematics Festival takes place on Whale Island. And, perhaps as an unofficial Oscars tie-in, it’s all about classic Hollywood filmmaking. Not only that, it also celebrates the aesthetics and industrial design of that era.

All around the game’s world, you’ll be able to find festival-themed collectables, which you can then use to unlock free Time-Limited Exhibition Passes.

If you log in during the event’s runtime, you’ll get the Car Cinema furniture set for free. This cosmetic bundle comes with chairs that are modelled after vintage vehicles, as well as poster display stands with unique movie making-themed decorations.

If you’re looking to spend some money, the Deluxe Festival Pack comes with a large Island Sunset Billboard, which you can place outside your home so everyone knows you spent that money. The same pack also comes with the Popcorn Movie Ticket chat bubble skin, and a 10% bonus to Festival Tokens when you sell stuff at the store.

Regardless of which pack you get, you’ll earn collection points for each, which puts you on the path to unlocking outfits like the Dreamlight Cinematics Festival-specific Modern Show Dandy and Modern Show Belle. There’s also a Cinematic Moments building material set launching with this event.

For now, we have the above reveal trailer to go on, which does offer some idea of what it’s going to look like in-game. Until things kick off on the weekend, you best arm yourself with some Heartopia codes.

#4173. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4172. Bandai Namco Reveals Its Involvement On Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Just recently, Xenoblade Chronicles developer Monolith Soft revealed its involvement on Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, confirming that it contributed to various aspects including "game design, programming, and graphics".

Monolith's involvement isn't a huge surprise given it's previous work on other Zelda titles, but another company has now spoken up to confirm its own involvement: Bandai Namco.

Taking to its official website, Bandai Namco revealed it helped out with various visual elements of the game ahead of its release on 5th November 2026:

"We were commissioned to create some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes, and UI, for the Nintendo Switch™ 2 game "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on November 5, 2026."

Of course, the primary developer for Ocarina of Time is Nintendo itself, with Hokwai Ng serving as director, with Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi on board as producers. We might be jumping the gun here, but we suspect Fujibayashi-san, who directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, is likely helming the next mainline game.

In a recent interview, Aonuma-san stated that the reason behind the assignment of HokWai Ng was his ability to "solve problems aggressively". He also presented some interesting ideas for future projects, prompting Aonuma to view him as the ideal candidate to helm Ocarina of Time.

#4171. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

#4170. Magic: The Gathering Gets Official Burger King Deck Box And Sleeves

Sam Woods is TheGamer’s Senior Reporter. He’s been in games journalism since 2020 and has undertaken a variety of roles in that time. These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He was promoted to the Senior Reporter position in 2025 following a series of high-quality reports and exclusives for TheGamer.

Since 2020, Sam has written over 3,000 articles and specializes in telling the stories of the people behind the games. He’s interviewed the biggest game directors, some of the industry’s top talents, told the stories of how indie games came to be, and spoken to players about what really makes them tick. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. He even hosted a PAX panel in 2021 and made a documentary in 2024 surrounding the creation of a Disney game.

Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. He got the scoop on Perfect Dark’s cancellation, provided context on some AI drama, and revealed that Lady Dimitrescu’s actress would love to step back into the character’s giant shoes. These articles have been picked up by the biggest gaming sites, including IGN, GameSpot, and PC Gamer. He also loves to dive into the numbers behind the games.

Sam’s journey in games journalism has taken him all over the world. He’s covered Gamescom in Germany, Summer Game Fest in Los Angeles, and Tokyo Game Show in Japan, each on three occasions.

He’s been learning Japanese since 2024 with the intention of identifying and translating Japanese-language news and bringing it to English-language audiences first, something he’s done countless times.

Sam’s first review was 2020’s Battletoads reboot, and he’s since reviewed games in The Legend of Zelda, Super Mario, and Pokemon franchises.

For years now, Pokemon Trading Card Game collectors have become accustomed to collaborations with McDonald's. Every year, the fast-food chain releases a series of cards with a special holographic pattern, limited to Happy Meals from the Golden Arches. In typical Pokemon fashion, recent promotions have caused carnage.

Magic: The Gathering has decided it has a little more class than collaborating with McDonald's; instead, it's teaming up with Burger King, where in one country, players can buy a special meal to get an exclusive Burger King-themed MTG Deck Box and Card Sleeves.

Burger King Italia has just released the Great Gathering Bundle. For €19.90 ($22.25), the bundle includes either a Krispper, Double Cheese King, or Whopper Plant-Based, plus 6 chicken bites, a box of fries, and a snazzy, slightly hilarious Burger King Deck Box and Card Sleeves.

The Deck Box and Sleeves bear the traditional Burger King orange and are designed to look like one of the chain's burgers. The box has sesame seeds on the front, with typical burger ingredients, like cheese, lettuce, and tomato, on the side. The promotion is available until November 30, if you fancy booking a quick trip to Italy.

Burger King joins an interesting couple of years of Magic: The Gathering collaborations. Although this is one-of-a-kind, the TCG has delved into a range of different franchises as part of its Secret Lair range, including Star Trek, Lo-Fi Girl, Hatsune Miku, and potentially soon KPop Demon Hunters.

With this promotion limited to a single country, calls have begun online, with people asking the Italian population to grab one for them. "Which of my great Italian friends is getting this beautiful BK deckbox for me?!?" said Matheus Vizos on Twitter. It's unlikely they'll have many takers, as, given the current state of TCGs, this sadly feels like a prime scalper opportunity.

#4168. 7 Soulslikes With the Most Nominations at The Game Awards

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Since 2009, FromSoftware has established an entire movement thanks to its work with the Soulsborne philosophy, not only giving us some of the best games of recent generations but also sparking the creativity of numerous developers worldwide.

The emergence of Soulslikes as a significant variation of ARPGs has been remarkable, influencing everyone from independent developers to major studios to follow in the footsteps of its challenging yet memorable journeys.

As more and more projects have joined the growing trend, the genre's average quality has increased considerably, which has been reflected in the ceremonies that celebrate each year's best titles.

Therefore, to remember which experiences have reached the pinnacle of recognition within the interactive industry, I present to you this list of the seven Soulslikes with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

Being not only the first great Soulslike game but also the first title to be nominated for a Game Awards category, Nioh is one of the genre's greatest representatives for many reasons.

Although it lost the Best Action Game award in 2017 to Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, Team Ninja took the first step in establishing what would eventually become the finest and most successful series in this subgenre.

Team Ninja was the first studio to place as much faith in the original formula as in its talent and expertise to create something uniquely its own while remaining instantly recognizable. The result was a devilishly challenging title with a remarkable personality that resonated with the community thanks to its profound experience.

The sequels would improve upon what was already quite enjoyable, although it's clear that the first Nioh is the installment with the most historical significance and contribution.

After 2017, we would have to wait three years before another Soulslike was represented at The Game Awards, which finally happened with Mortal Shell's nomination for Best Debut Game.

Following Nioh's unfortunate trajectory, Cold Symmetry's project fell victim to the Phasmophobia phenomenon, though its achievement's magnitude was still considerable, not only given its independent status but also its significance in a niche genre.

Even without reaching its most refined version, which would come with the sequel, the title already possessed enough authority and ambition to be featured at the industry's most prestigious awards ceremony, a truly remarkable feat.

Currently, Mortal Shell might seem slightly outdated, more so considering the comprehensive improvements offered by its successor, yet this shouldn't detract from the fact that it was one of the best-received Soulslikes upon its release.

A list of ten soulslike games where the player turns out to be the villain by the end.

For the second time in a row, Team Ninja had to watch the Best Action Game award slip through their fingers, with the category going to Hades instead of Nioh 2.

Despite the comprehensive improvements the sequel added, it wasn't able to secure more submissions than the one it had received years earlier, partly because many preferred the original's darker, more focused, and less cluttered style.

Regardless of the reasons, and even though it was among 2020's standout titles, the studio had to settle for repeating the milestone, though it's more significant than it might seem considering that the IP now accounted for two-thirds of the genre's all-time nominations.

Certainly, two out of three is nominally a small number, but for a type of game that, by definition, will never achieve mainstream success, it's a clear demonstration of the IP's stature.

The genre suffered another defeat in 2021 with Death's Door, a practically 'Soulslite' approach that, nevertheless, remains one of the current decade’s best action-adventure titles.

In the Best Independent Game category, Acid Nerve's creation succumbed to Kena: Bridge of Spirits, but it did so surrounded by absolute marvels of the indie ecosystem, such as Inscryption and Loop Hero, demonstrating that the level of competition was extremely high.

Death's Door, like Hollow Knight in 2017, belongs to that lighter variant of the genre that focuses on concepts and ideas rather than strict mechanics, and the result was a hybrid between The Legend of Zelda and Dark Souls that feels truly majestic.

It may not have won, but Titan Souls' creators made a tremendous leap in quality by moving from the iconic boss rush to this fully-fledged adventure, which continues to be a regular fixture on lists of the best experiences of its kind.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

Remnant: From the Ashes surprised the world with its magnificent combination of Soulslike mechanics, third-person shooter gameplay, and multiplayer, while Remnant 2 refined the package and capitalized on that success.

In 2023, the Best Action Game category once again featured a genre standard-bearer, though it had to face the bittersweet reality of defeat, particularly at the hands of FromSoftware and Armored Core 6: Fires of Rubicon.

However, after a 2022 in which only FromSoftware made an appearance at the event, returning to the biggest stage in video games was important enough to maintain the genre's vitality.

Remnant 2's success is undeniable, but so are the frustrations of a genre that, after more than five years of accumulating nominations, had yet to secure even a single award that would elevate it to a new level.

Lies of P made Soulslike history in 2023 by becoming the first game in the subgenre to receive more than one nomination, an achievement unmatched until then.

Round8 Studio and NEOWIZ emerged from absolute obscurity and yet released what I consider the best Soulslike ever made, not only perfectly emulating FromSoftware's work but also imbuing it with a recognizable and well-developed identity.

It lost Best RPG to Baldur's Gate 3 and Best Art Direction to Alan Wake 2, but considering that both were Game of the Year nominees and consistently rank among the decade's best games, there's little to criticize about Lies of P.

Unfortunately, the game's quality and refinement remain an anomaly that exceeds the genre's actual average, though it continues to be a benchmark for future Soulslikes aspiring to such heights.

There's nothing more fitting for this season than being destroyed by the same boss fifty-seven times in a row.

However, the biggest historical event for Soulslikes at The Game Awards came in 2024 with Black Myth: Wukong, by far the most acclaimed game in the genre from the specialized press.

With the highest number of nominations ever recorded at The Game Awards, the genre's only Game of the Year nomination, and the sole winner of a medal (two, actually), Game Science shattered all previous standards for Soulsborne heirs.

Its nominations for GOTY, Best Game Direction, Best Art Direction, Best Action Game, and Players' Voice were historic, as were its conquests over the latter two categories, cementing its place in the annals of Soulslikes.

One of its victories was in the popular vote's realm, the particular category decided entirely by users and not the specialized media, although it doesn't diminish the merit of a production that paved the way for a whole country.

Since its resounding success, China has opened up beyond the mobile market to continue capitalizing on Black Myth: Wukong's prosperity, positioning it as a giant whose shoulders carry an entire ecosystem thanks to its distinctive excellence.

If you're looking for the heir to Soulsborne games, look no further than this list of ten Soulslikes that are unexpected masterpieces.

#4167. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

#4166. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4165. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

#4164. PlayStation Cancels Haven Studios' Debut Title Fairgames

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Live service titles are a double-edged sword, both for the developers working on them and the greater industry as a whole. While the promise of constant support and almost endless content sounds incredibly promising, the strain and repetition lead to many titles that attempt the feat crashing and burning, oftentimes before they really get off the ground.

After a nearly 4-year wait, macOS fans of Relic's Company of Heroes franchise will finally get to play the most recent entry.

Back in 2023, Sony announced a myriad of live service titles aimed to help the studio earn a spot in the active multiplayer space, many of which have petered out pre- and post-launch. Fairgames joins the list of canceled games, officially canceled after lackluster numbers in player tests. Despite this decision, Sony claims no employees will be laid off, offering a silver lining amid another live service disaster.

Usually, failed live service titles lead to major consequences, as their nature requires mountains of work and advertising to really get off the ground. Not only do they need substantial content in the initial launch, but plenty ready to go in order to tide players over as weeks and months pass by. Concord, Redfall, even successes like Destiny 2 tend to stumble before getting snuffed out with a whimper.

Usually this means jobs lost and talented developers ousted, but Sony is making the great call to keep everyone working at Haven Studios on, instead shifting them to support other active development projects across PlayStation’s catalog before letting them pursue their own creative output again.

While the promise of constant support and almost endless content sounds incredibly promising, the strain and repetition lead to many titles that attempt the feat crashing and burning, oftentimes before they really get off the ground.

Sony made it clear through an internal email release that the issue wasn’t the quality of Haven Studios’ work, but the incredibly saturated online live-service shooter market. Titans like Overwatch, Call of Duty, and Marvel Rivals make it incredibly difficult to get a foot in the door, despite the “strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement” Haven Studios managed to put together.

With the failure of most of Sony’s live service initiatives, it’s a bit comforting to see them not lash out at the devs who tried to make a bad plan work, and instead pivot to projects that hopefully have a bit sturdier legs to stand on. Their single-player titles have easily been the platform’s strongest selling point, and focusing on what they know works will do wonders to earn back public support.

After the announcement of their redoubled efforts to keep Sony games on PlayStation, it feels like Sony is aiming to tighten up their ship a bit, forgoing some of their more haphazard programs to hone in on what people come to PlayStation for: strong, single-player titles with truly unique gameplay. Spider-Man, Horizon, and Ghost of Yotei are recent successes that are the real reason Sony still has a place.

With the rise and constant fear of studio closures and layoffs, Sony needs to keep their ship tight, rewarding longtime devs while inviting new blood in for opportunities to show their stuff. Otherwise, they could continue to stagnate in the console space, allowing Nintendo to pull even further ahead. Sony’s real rival, Xbox, is in a similar rut, and digging their way out would be a great way to surge ahead.

While the odd live-service title may find its niche audience, they often require numbers that are nigh impossible to maintain over any extended period. Titles like Marvel Rivals and Call of Duty have ridiculous numbers of constantly paying customers, a situation that is much harder to replicate than many would have you believe.

With Fairgames gone, Haven Studios has another chance to define itself, even if that only starts as support for bigger teams. A debut title can make or break a studio, and if Fairgames crashed and burned, I don’t think Haven would have lasted much longer.

#4163. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

#4162. Rumour: Samsung's New Chip Process Kicks Off 'Nintendo Switch 2 Lite' Speculation

Update: Digital Foundry weighs in on the rumour

Update [Mon 9th Nov 2026, 4:45pm]: At the end of last month, we covered a rumour that Nintendo was working on a 'Switch 2 Lite' model that would supposedly utilise a new chip process in the works at Samsung.

We clarified at the time that it was all nothing more than a rumour, and now the tech experts over at Digital Foundry have popped up to add their ten cents' worth to the conversation. Unsurprisingly, they don't have a whole lot of faith in the idea.

The biggest reason for the outlet's dismissal is the lack of any solid sourcing that Nintendo is looking to downsize its hardware in the first place. "The existence of Samsung materials for a new process that could be used for a handheld doesn't say much on its own," DF says, claiming that the rumoured specs look "more like guesswork".

Then there's the technical side of things, with DF noting that Switch 2 already uses a bespoke processor, so it's not like the transition to the new 8LPU+ would come easily. On top of that, it deems the chip process' rumoured 15% drop in power consumption as "nice to have, but doesn't yield the transformative battery improvements required for a smaller revision" — the original jump from Switch to Switch Lite roughly halved power consumption, let's not forget.

Still, the rumour remains exactly that, a rumour, for the time being. Samsung should spill the beans on the new process next month, but until then, it might be best to continue taking everything with a pinch of salt.

News Is Switch 2 Lite Possible, Thanks to New Samsung Chip Technology?

Digital FoundrySpecs have appeared online, but something doesn't make sense.

Original Story: Samsung reportedly has a new chip in the works that could help make dreams of a 'Switch 2 Lite' a reality (thanks for the heads up, Notebook Check).

As shared on Bluesky by Nintendo Patents Watch, Samsung has supposedly been working on a new 8LPU+ chip process which might be able to assist with making the Nvidia chip inside Switch 2 more compact and more powerful, while drawing on less power.

While the chip itself hasn't been officially revealed yet (South Korean outlet Electronic Times reports that it could be unveiled in December), the word on the street is that the chip process will boast a 12% performance enhancement, 15% power reduction, and an 8% area shrink, among other features, making it a prime candidate for, we don't know, a smaller console.

At the IEDM 2026, Samsung is scheduled to present its 2nd-gen 8nm process 8LPU+: • 12% performance enhancement • 15% power reduction • 8% area shrink • ~10% I/O area reduction • Stand-by leakage reduction Is this Nvidia and Nintendo’s plan all along for the Switch 2 Lite? 1/

With Samsung behind the custom Nvidia chip already in the Switch 2, there's every chance that the new tech could also be used in Nintendo's favour. A smaller Switch 2 — perhaps borrowing the portable-first, non-dock USPs of its predecessor's Lite model — might even pose a cheaper alternative for those wanting to get in on the new hardware's exclusives. With rising costs on just about everything (particularly in the tech space), a less powerful Switch 2 model with cheaper components sure does sound appealing.

We've also got to remember that Nintendo is wrapping up Switch 1 distribution in February 2027. It doesn't necessarily mean that something will be coming in to replace it, we should point out, but if Nintendo and Samsung do have something in the works, it'd be a prime time to introduce it. Heck, the original Switch Lite was released a mere two and a half years after the base model, so who's to say Nintendo doesn't have a Switch 2 equivalent in store for late 2028?

Of course, we've already seen the smallest Switch 2 revision already this year, with the replaceable battery model being introduced in Europe. Rumblings of an 'OLED model' remain under the surface as ever, but what if a 'Lite' option pops up first? Only time will tell, eh!

#4161. Grand Theft Auto VI Will Run At 30 FPS On All Consoles, But PS5 Pro Will Feature 'Improved Clarity' And Ray-Traced Shadows

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19, and you can preload the game on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S starting today, Rockstar Games has announced. The studio has also revealed what kind of visuals players can expect on their respective consoles, making clear that regardless of where you play, GTA VI targets 30 FPS gameplay.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life – while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants," Rockstar writes in a blog post.

Rockstar Games also breaks down the different graphical settings available on PlayStation and Xbox consoles. On PS5 Pro, GTA VI will feature "improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro." On PS5 and PS5 Pro, the game will include "high-fidelity haptic feedback" fully integrated into DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D audio, and improved load times, "making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles."

On Xbox consoles, Rockstar doesn't dive into performance; instead, it focuses on Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One consoles, noting this feature will use Xbox Series S graphics settings.

GTA VI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. After that, check out this exclusive story about how GTA VI features over 170 animal species and another about its tropical storms and hurricanes.

Where will you play GTA VI? Let us know in the comments below!

#4160. Here Is Every Commander Deck From 2026 Ranked From Worst To Best

Magic: The Gathering set is all wrapped up for 2026 after the launch of the Star Trek set and its four Commander precons, which have added to an already strong Universes Beyond pool this year. We do still have an unconfirmed Spider-Man Commander precon in December, but we're still waiting on more details.

That brings us to 25 unique Commander precon decks so far this year, so we're going to look back at every deck we've had the pleasure of playingand rank them from worst to best.

If you love picking up Commander precons with each new set, we've got great news, as there will be at least four precons per set next year, meaning at least 24 new precons are coming in 2027.

Updated on November 10, 2026, by Niall Walsh: We're adding the Star Trek Commander precons to this list, having had the chance to play with them over the prerelease week and put them through their paces against a number of different precons from this year.

While there are easily no terrible Commander precons from 2026 so far, one of these decks has to come in last place, and for me, it's Blight Curse.

I don't mind the Blight mechanic at all, but it's barely made an impact on Standard play, and this deck just isn't quite on the same level as many of the others released so far this year.

Blight Curse is currently worth $44.40 according to TCGPlayer.

I've played with and against this deck, and it's always struggled to keep up with the pace of the game and to have any meaningful impact. If anything, it churns away and drags games out, if only because it's the lowest threat at the table and gets treated as such.

That said, it can be quite the engine if you leave Auntie, Ool, and Cursewretch unchecked on the battlefield. Blighting creatures impact the game no matter what, either by drawing cards or by making opponents lose 1 life.

Still, it's an unremarkable deck that could use major upgrades, and some of the cards released in The Hobbit make that easier and more impactful if you want to turn it into a consistent performer at your local game night.

We take a look at the very best MTG precon decks for the Commander format.

I'm not a fan of Planeswalker-led Commander decks at the best of times, and while Lorehold Spirit can still pop off for big damage as you swing wide with Spirit tokens, it's a fairly one-dimensional deck that can be easily frustrated.

This deck is built on the Boros Flashback mechanic and general graveyard interactions. The idea is to cast spells that can be cast again from your graveyard or ones that let you manipulate your graveyard in any way. In doing so, you'll also create Spirit 3/2 tokens.

The Lorehold Spirit deck is worth $60.87 according to TCGPlayer.

The main issue I have with the deck is that any half-decent Commander player will see what this deck is trying to achieve from miles away and just reserve removal, board wipes, and graveyard exiles to repeatedly hammer down on its controller until they're left with few strategic options.

Boros tends to do better in Standard because it's one-on-one and 20 life points. You can play as aggressively as you like, and the game's limited nature often means you can overwhelm your opponent before they have a decent answer. In Commander, games naturally go on for much longer, and a deck like this gets weaker with every turn if its battlefield isn't stacked with powerful creatures and tokens.

This is one of two decks that it hurts to have so low down this ranking, but Witherbloom Pestilence just isn't as powerful as I hoped it would be, especially when this Strixhaven College is arguably the best to use in the Limited format, and has seen multiple cards cross over into the Standard meta for some fringe decks.

The deck is far too creature-heavy, with 39 in total, which is somewhat understandable given there will be a lot of sacrificing, but that's typically reserved for tokens created by instants, sorceries, and enchantments. Basically, the deck feels unbalanced, and if players know your strategy is to go all in on creatures, they'll be more aware of your combos and more keen to stop them.

The Witherbloom Pestilence deck is worth $63.52 according to TCGPlayer.

I would argue that this is one of the better decks on this list for new players, as its creature-heavy nature is good for learning about combos, synergies, and how dynamic certain creatures can be, but if you hope to make it truly competitive at your game night, it's going to take quite a few upgrades.

Admittedly, I struggle with where to rank the Turtle Power deck on this list. Looking at it from a pure power perspective, it's relatively high up. The option to run a Partner Commander is also a big plus, as is the wonderful thematic storytelling behind its design. However, it just doesn't consistently become the giant mutant engine it should be.

It's a slow starter if you don't have a curated first hand, and I would say that it's such a situational deck that even pulling generally good cards off the top of your deck can feel a little jarring when you haven't got your board set up right to play and/or protect it.

The Turtle Power deck is worth $81.67 according to TCGPlayer.

WUBRG decks are always a little tricky to judge if they're not blatantly powerful right out of the box, and because the theming of this deck is so cool, it feels disruptive to try and make upgrades to it, so it's almost a case of being a precon that you shouldn't upgrade, but yet it desperately needs it.

Ultimately, I compare this deck with the other WUBRG that has been released this year, and in doing so, it became much clearer where the two stack up against each other and the rest of this list, and Turtle Power falls into the lower half as a result.

Some aggro decks are just built better than others, and Klingon Fury has so much potential as an idea, but the end product doesn't quite live up to the bill. This feels like a deck that should be pumping out Klingon tokens and low-cost Klingon creatures, supported by burn spells and ways to increase the power of a specific creature type. This is there to some extent, but it doesn't fully commit to the idea the way Goblin Storm does, and it ends up being far slower than it should be.

A five-mana Commander doesn't help, either, and while there are ways to get some ramp to cast him on turn three, you're in "planets aligning" territory to get there reliably over and over.

It's far from a bad deck, but if you're looking for quick, clean wins, this deck isn't that, and it requires a little more work to get everything to come together and reach a dangerous board state.

We follow one Star Trek deck up with another, as Federation Fleet falls into the bottom half of decks released this year. Like so many others on this list, it's far from bad, and with the right starting hand it's brilliant, but as a consistent performer, it struggles, and the split strategy of big powerful creatures and the flying threat of Spacecrafts just clashes a little too much.

This deck relies on card draw and counter distribution, and the Seek Out ability has some huge activations that can turn a game on its head if used right, but the setup required to reach that point will likely see you identified as a threat pretty early on, and you'll rarely get to pull off any of your exciting and dangerous combos.

This deck would have benefited from being a little more adventurous with its theming and focusing a little less on Seek Out. Despite it being very easy to trigger the second card draw each turn, the triggers pile up, and it can become a chore to work through them all each time, and not all of them have any impact on your opponents.

This is the other deck that pains me to have this low, but Doom Prevails is just ripe for upgrades and never quite gets over the line to reach its potential straight out of the box.

Conniving is the name of the game with this deck, but the creatures sometimes don't mesh well with the strategy, and instead it gets a little lost, especially if you can't get good Connive cards on the board early on. Doctor Doom lets Connive benefit you no matter the outcome: when you discard a land card, each opponent takes 2 damage, and if it's a nonland card, you still put a +1/+1 counter on the creature that Connived. But without some truly repetitive Connive triggers, this isn't as powerful as it first seems.

The Doom Prevails deck is worth $93.03 according to TCGPlayer.

Black Market Connections is also a big part of the deck, and getting it onto the board early, but still struggling to put some of the combos together, just results in the deck bleeding you dry of life points while your opponents sit and laugh.

Upgrades can make this deck very good, but without that refinement, it's a little hit-and-miss, so it can't quite crack the top half of this ranking.

We're getting into the decks that are largely separated by fine margins now, with Wakanda Forever being a very good artifacts deck that just focuses a little too much on mana artifacts for my liking.

Given how T'Challa works, you won't be short on colorless mana to cast artifacts, yet a quarter of the 24 artifacts in this deck are mana generators. Beyond the basic Arcane Signet and Sol Ring, artifacts that produce mana feel wasted in this deck, so it could have leaned harder into card draw, equipment, or vehicles to really power up this strategy.

The Wakanda Forever deck is worth $84.23 according to TCGPlayer.

The instant and sorcery spells in this deck could also use some refinement. It has the expected removal and looting, but I would like to see more token generation or boosting for existing creatures to add another deadly element to the playbook.

Finally, 12 forests and 12 plains leave plenty of room for more powerful or impactful lands, which feels like an obvious starting point for upgrades.

What this deck does well, however, is stick to its core artifact-based attack, and it can become a problem very quickly if you get T'Challa churning out the Vibranium tokens as soon as possible.

Okay, so the Foundations starter decks are actually a whole lot better than I thought. Each of the five mono-color decks brings a ton of value to the table, not necessarily in the cards, but in how it teaches the basic principles of Commander as a format, while still making it incredibly fun. Oh, and each deck is competitive, too. You won't need to upgrade these decks to earn your first win in casual settings, and that arguably makes them the perfect starting block for anyone new to the format.

It's been ages since the last Commander starter decks were released, and the game has changed a lot in that time. I wasn't initially a fan of these decks being mono-color, but after reading through the decklists, it's the right play.

Taking everything into account, these are great Commander decks to start your journey with, especially for under $30, and if not for the quality of precon we've seen this year, they would have ranked much higher.

While the hype for the Hatsune Miku Secret Lair deck may have been high, when you take a step back and really look at the deck, it's nothing special, not in the same way that Goblin Storm was such an obvious win.

That said, Trostani, Selesnya's Voice is an interesting Commander who works well in token, Populate, Lifelink, and +1/+1 counter decks, and this deck list has a little bit of everything.

The Hatsune Miku deck has a market value of $447.21, according to TCGPlayer.

Taking almost the opposite approach to Goblin Storm, this Secret Lair precon is less about winning and more about having fun, so bear that in mind if you pick one up.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4159. Caleb's third Myth has finally arrived in Love and Deepspace, and it's good news for all the husbandbro fans out there

Love and Deepspace has kicked off a new event, squarely built around Caleb's new Memory Pair.

Love and Deepspace’s latest update is here, adding a new Memory Pair for Caleb. The event is dubbed Ghosts' Final March, and it’s available now as part of a new Limited Wish Pool, as it has always worked.

The new Memory Pair is a 5-Star Solar-Slot, which can be obtained through the aforementioned Wish Pool. Doing so will unlock the Netherlord Companion for Caleb, and there’s even more for you to explore in this one.

Alongside the big new Memory Pair, Ghosts' Final March also offers the opportunity to earn a new 4-Star Solar-Slot Memory Pair, alongside ten Deepspace Wishes, 500 Diamonds, and other freebies. The event ends on April 11, so you have some time to get in and play.

If you’re only interested in the 5-Star variants, you’ll be happy to know that Infold is sticking with 150 pulls as the absolute maximum to guarantee earning Netherlord. This will be automatically unlocked after you pull both Nether Yearning and Nether Parting through the Wish Pool.

Obtaining either of the two will give you access to all chapters for the new Myth that’s also available as part of this event: Yin Yang Sundering. You can read all the lore once either of the two Memories have been unlocked, and you won’t even need to upgrade either of them.

The Lost Souls event has also kicked off alongside the new update. You can take part to claim a 4-Star Solar Slor Memory Pair for Caleb: Duskshard Dreams and Duskshard Lotus. You can also earn the 3-Star Memory, Lotus Bond, alongside some other freebies like more Wishes, Diamonds, Photo Poses, and an event-exclusive title.

After you unlock Caleb’s Netherlord Companion, you may want to fight alongside him to get another 4-Star Memory for free. You’ll need to challenge the the Rehearsal Stage to do so, and your first clear is guaranteed to get you the Duskshard Lotus Memory.

If you’re new to Love and Deepspace, or you simply want a refresher, we’ve put together a guide to help you wrap your head around Myths; how they work and how to unlock them. Banners are also an important part of any gacha game, Love and Deepspace included, so here’s how banners work, and what the current and next banners are.

And, as ever, it’s worth checking if you’re missing any of these Love and Deepspace codes to get some in-game freebies.

#4158. Update: You Can Preload Grand Theft Auto VI On PS5 and Xbox Today, And You Should Because It's Massive

Rockstar Games revealed last week that players can preload Grand Theft Auto VI on their console of choice the following week, and that time has arrived. The studio released a blog post today to announce that you can preload GTA VI on PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S. If you're excited about the game, you will probably want to go ahead and do this because it will take up a whopping 212 GB of space on your drives – make the room now so you don't hit this roadblock next week when the game goes live on Thursday, November 19.

The blog post also details performance on PlayStation and Xbox consoles, and you can read more about what to expect here.

We're just over two weeks away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which recently graced the cover of Game Informer. Ahead of its November 19 launch, Rockstar Games has announced that digital preloading for GTA VI will begin next week on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

More specifically, preloading on Xbox Series X/S will begin Tuesday, November 10, at 12 a.m. GMT (4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on November 9), and on PS5 at midnight local time in your time zone. Although Rockstar isn't producing physical discs of GTA VI, you can still buy a physical box at retail, which includes a download code for the game. The studio says, "Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12."

The preload file will require 212 GB on your device, so make sure you have the space before you start the download. You can find more details about this process here.

Elsewhere in today's GTA VI news, Rockstar has revealed that on November 19, it will add an official printable GTA VI cover art poster and a map of Leonida as a free digital download to the game's official site. However, a double-sided physical version of this poster will be made available shortly after the launch of GTA VI from the Rockstar Store. It will only cost $0.99 on its own, or come free with any other purchase from the store.

#4157. Poll: Which Zelda: Ocarina Of Time HUD Option Is Your Favourite?

Just like the open-world entries that precede it, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 comes with a handful of HUD options, so you can play with as much or as little on-screen information as you please.

In our first few hours with the game, we played around with all three of these options, getting to grips with the pros and cons of all of them. Most of us settled on one after a little while, and now we're keen to see where you lovely lot have ended up.

As a reminder, there are three different HUD options in the settings menu's 'In-Game Interface Tab': Normal, Pro, and Master. The first of these is listed as your "Standard display," with your mini map, item selection, D-pad options, life/magic meters, and button prompts all appearing on the screen. It offers the most information you can get at a glance, but it can look a little cluttered for some.

The 'Pro' option tones things down a little, displaying "minimal information," according to its settings definition. This one does away with almost all the info we mentioned above, but button prompts (for 'Talk' or 'Grab' selections) and Navi's speech bubbles still make an appearance. This is a ripe choice for anyone who knows their Zelda mechanics, but still wants to know when something is there to be interacted with.

'Master' mode is the most stripped back of the bunch, offering a "display with no information". This means that everything other than the main gameplay is removed from the screen, and no prompts crop up as you approach NPCs or interactive items. And yes, that includes your targeting cursor. This option keeps things stripped back to the bare minimum and arguably provides the most immersive experience of the bunch, but there's every chance that you'll miss the odd detail (or Navi quip) along the way.

Each setting has its perks, to be sure, and we're not about to say that any one of them is the 'correct' way to play, but still, we're interested to know what mode you have been rocking with so far.

You can let us know your preferred HUD option in the following poll, then take to the comments to let us know why it's stuck.

Which option have you been maining? Let us know in the comments.

#4156. The Petit Planet beta is coming back with new updates, but you still need to hope for an invite

If you've been missing Petit Planet since it was last available to play, you'll be happy to know that HoYoverse is hosting another test soon.

It’s been quite a while since we’ve heard anything about Petit Planet, the upcoming game from Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail developer HoYoverse. By most accounts, Petit Planet is the studio’s take on Animal Crossing, though with a few interesting ideas of its own.

The game’s most recent test took place all the way back in November, but its next big test isn’t far off.

HoYoverse announced today that Petit Planet’s Stardrift Test is scheduled for April 21. This latest build will be available on PC, Android, and iOS. The beta will include new Neighbors, an updated Starsea Voyage, and more for you to do at the Galactic Bazaar.

Seeing as interacting with Neighbors is a core part of this life sim RPG, the confirmation that new faces will be available in this test is big news. Each Neighbor in Petit Planet is a character, with their own personalty and life story.

The Starsea Voyage now includes a map, too, which you can use to take you to other Islets. If you played any of the previous tests, you should already be familiar with this feature.

The only bit of bad news here is that this remains a closed beta. You’re still encouraged to sign up on the official website, but you’re not guaranteed access. HoYoverse said that only a portion of players who sign up will be invited to the upcoming beta.

Petit Planet remains without a release date. If nothing else, it’ll be interesting to see the progress the game has made since last November’s beta.

#4155. House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

Big Walk developer House House has found itself at the center of a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival on March 3, 2027, after a group of its jurors said they would not vote for any game that has used generative AI in any capacity. The jurors' statement does not name House House or Big Walk, but the studio eventually updated its FAQ to explain how it used generative AI for coding after IGF discussions. After vaguely posting on social media, those associated with IGF made clear that a sticking point in the voting process was Big Walk.

Former games journalist and game developer Austin Walker posted the IGF jurors' statement on Bluesky, explaining that voting has been difficult this year due to the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools."

"This has set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools, and at this point there is no universal consensus on what (if anything) is to be done," the statement reads. "The IGF has affirmed that we may cast our votes according to our own tastes and values. But we, as a contingent of IGF jurors, feel that this trend and the games embracing it deserve stronger pushback than a vote in silence."

The statement continues, explaining that not all jurors are on board with the blanket statement, citing reasons including "their ability to safely sign without professional blowback." It continues, "Above all: Our goal is to state solidarity with those who despair over the future of their art, their craft, and their industry – including those who have experimented with these tools, but who now believe they are not in our best interest."

The statement continues with the jurors' beliefs regarding gen-AI, including its negative effects, that any gen-AI used in any process of game development is not okay, noting specifically that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms," and more.

"For those reasons, this year we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity," the statement says. "We urge the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work." The statement then includes the names of the IGF jurors who signed it.

Big Walk isn't specifically mentioned within that statement. However, Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming IGF, tells Aftermath that "it got to the point where the most-discussed game this year almost entirely involved its AI usage, overshadowing pretty much everything else." LeClair says it felt like a boiling point, adding, "Anyhow, strong props to the jurors for taking this stance and putting out this letter as well, even if some people believe that using AI for coding purposes is a more gray area, we're at a point where the amount of AI slop clogging up the indie game scene means having to take hard stances such as this in order to discourage such an amount of recklessness."

Again, no mention of Big Walk. However, game developer Bruno Diaz took to BlueSky to confirm the speculation: that most-discussed game was Big Walk. "Okay, because the cat is out of the f---ing bag, I might as well combat misinformation a bit: 1. The reason IGF judges are aware of the LLM use in the development of Big Walk is through a disclosure shared by House House. 2. This disclosure was required by IGF rules. 3. While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly 'consultative' use and not code gen or agents."

Diaz notes that they believe that distinction is without a difference, adding that "to my knowledge, it is not the case that Big Walk is non-compliant with the former [Steam's AI disclosure requirements]."

"Yes, there was a large discussion about this in internal IGF forums," Diaz said. "Yes, a lot of people said things that I personally think were disingenuous, extremely disappointing, or just (frankly) dumb. No, I have no intention of talking about it in further detail or exposing anyone. [...] Ultimately, it is extremely difficult for a group of over 100 people to keep a secret so I expected this to come out eventually. Shrug emoji. If you think something is reputationally damaging, consider not doing it."

With discussion surrounding Big Walk happening during the IGF discussions, House House updated its FAQ to address, "Was AI used to make Big Walk?" Here's what the FAQ reads, in full:

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you can see, House House did not disclose its use of AI-generated code because "Steam as a platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage." It says it is posting the disclosure now as "it has become a matter of public interest."

House House recently made headlines for choosing not to put Big Walk on Xbox in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft Games. Earlier this year, it gained widespread critical acclaim for its unique emphasis on cooperative puzzle-solving – you can read more about that in Game Informer's Big Walk review.

#4154. Heartopia celebrates 30 million downloads with new outfits, permanent price cuts

Heartopia's rise has continued since its launch earlier this year, and the game's developer isn't slowing down with updates.

Heartopia has kicked off a new event to celebrate passing 30 million downloads. Just a couple of weeks after delivering the vintage Hollywood-themed Dreamlight Cinematics event, developer XD Games has revealed The Whimsical Tea Party, a limited-time Gilded Acorn Exhibition.

The event kicked off on Saturday, bringing some new themed content to the game.

Whimsical Tea Party’s biggest addition are the new outfits, including the Wandering Traveler, and the Duke Bunny outfits. Each outfit is available in three different colours. Another thing Heartopia events bring are building materials sets.

This one adds the Labyrinth furniture building materials set, the Hedgehog & Flamingo mallet, and the Cheshire Cat pet costume. Speaking of outfits, XD Games is dropping the in-game prices for a number of items permanently.

All original pet outfits now cost 66.7% less. Those of the Common variety will now cost 10 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, instead of the previous 30. Rare pet outfits will cost 5 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, down from 15.

If you happened to buy Common or Rare original pet outfits between July 17, 2024 and March 22, 2026, you’ll be refunded the difference.
